Environment & Sustainability — Study Notes & Diagrams

Unit 1 — Environment, Atmosphere and Sustainable Development

CO1 · Q1–Q20
Q01

Define environment, sustainability, and human-environment interaction.

L1
Definition
Environment is everything living and non-living around us; sustainability is meeting today's needs without harming future generations; human-environment interaction is how people depend on, adapt to, and modify nature.
Key Point
These three concepts form the foundation of the course because every human action alters natural systems that we rely on to survive.
Example
Farming fertile river plains, building dams for irrigation, and planting shelterbelt trees to stop soil erosion.
Q02

Define the atmosphere and explain its importance to the Earth.

L2
Definition
The atmosphere is the protective blanket of gases—mainly 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen—held around Earth by gravity.
Key Point
It supplies breathable air, shields life from harmful radiation and meteoroids, drives the water cycle, and prevents extreme day-night temperature swings.
Example
Without an atmosphere like Earth's, our planet would resemble the Moon, swinging from scorching heat in sunlight to freezing cold at night.
Q03

Describe the major layers of the atmosphere and state the key feature of each.

L2
Definition
The atmosphere is divided by temperature into five layers: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere, and exosphere.
Key Point
Weather happens in the troposphere, the ozone layer sits in the stratosphere, meteors burn in the mesosphere, auroras glow in the thermosphere, and satellites orbit in the exosphere.
Example
Commercial airplanes cruise near the top of the troposphere or lower stratosphere to stay above turbulent storm clouds.
Q04

Explain the role of the atmosphere in regulating Earth's temperature.

L2
Definition
Atmospheric temperature regulation is the balance between incoming solar radiation and outgoing heat kept steady by air circulation and trace gases.
Key Point
Clouds and bright surfaces reflect excess sunlight by day, while greenhouse gases trap outgoing infrared heat at night so Earth stays habitable around 15°C on average.
Example
Coastal cities like Mumbai have milder temperature swings than dry deserts because humid atmospheric air holds heat more evenly.
Q05

Explain the significance of the ozone layer for life on Earth.

L2
Definition
The ozone layer is a concentrated band of ozone gas (O₃) in the stratosphere, roughly 15 to 35 km above Earth's surface.
Key Point
It absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet-B (UV-B) radiation, protecting DNA, human skin, eyes, crops, and marine plankton.
Example
Think of the ozone layer as Earth's natural sunscreen—without it, skin cancer rates and cataract cases would surge worldwide.
Q06

Describe the causes and consequences of ozone layer depletion.

L2
Definition
Ozone depletion is the thinning of the stratospheric ozone shield caused by man-made ozone-depleting substances.
Key Point
Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and halons release chlorine and bromine atoms that break apart ozone molecules, letting more UV-B reach Earth and harming human health and ecosystems.
Example
Old refrigerators and aerosol sprays using CFCs caused the Antarctic ozone hole, which is now slowly recovering thanks to the Montreal Protocol.
Q07

Differentiate between weather and climate.

L4
Definition
Weather is the short-term state of the atmosphere over hours or days, while climate is the long-term average weather pattern over 30 years or more.
Key Point
Weather changes rapidly and locally, whereas climate defines a region's expected seasons and shifts slowly over decades.
Example
A rainy afternoon in Pune is weather; Pune's recurring June-to-September monsoon season is climate.
Q08

Explain the greenhouse effect and its role in maintaining Earth's temperature.

L2
Definition
The greenhouse effect is the natural warming process where gases like CO₂, water vapor, and methane trap outgoing infrared heat in the lower atmosphere.
Key Point
In natural amounts, it keeps Earth about 33°C warmer than a frozen rock; however, excess human emissions amplify it into global warming.
Example
Just like a parked car heats up when sunlight passes through the windshield and heat stays trapped inside, Earth's atmosphere retains warmth.
Q09

Define sustainable development and explain its importance.

L2
Definition
Sustainable development is progress that satisfies present human needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
Key Point
It matters because natural resources are finite; unchecked growth exhausts water, soil, and forests and deepens inequality.
Example
Harvesting timber only at the rate new trees grow back ensures both jobs today and healthy forests tomorrow.
Q10

Explain the three pillars of sustainable development with examples.

L3
Definition
The three pillars are environmental protection, economic growth, and social equity—often remembered as Planet, Profit, and People.
Key Point
True sustainability only works when all three pillars are balanced together rather than sacrificing one for another.
Example
A solar-powered rural clinic cuts carbon emissions (planet), lowers electricity bills (profit), and delivers healthcare to villagers (people).
Q11

Describe the relationship between environmental protection and economic development.

L2
Definition
Environment and economy are interdependent: nature provides the raw materials, clean water, and stable climate that every industry depends on.
Key Point
Short-term pollution may look cheap, but environmental damage creates huge healthcare, disaster, and resource-scarcity costs later.
Example
Investing in clean solar manufacturing creates green jobs and exports while reducing costly coal-pollution health bills.
Q12

Explain human-environment interaction with positive examples.

L2
Definition
Positive human-environment interaction occurs when human actions restore ecosystems, conserve resources, and support biodiversity.
Key Point
Thoughtful planning and stewardship can heal degraded land and improve both nature and human livelihoods.
Example
Community reforestation drives, rainwater harvesting pits, and protected wildlife sanctuaries like Kaziranga National Park.
Q13

Explain human-environment interaction with negative examples.

L2
Definition
Negative human-environment interaction happens when human activities degrade air, water, soil, or habitats faster than nature can recover.
Key Point
Overexploitation, pollution, and unplanned land clearing disrupt ecological balance and trigger disasters like floods or droughts.
Example
Deforestation for unregulated mining, dumping untreated factory wastewater into rivers, and single-use plastic littering.
Q14

Differentiate between biotic and abiotic components of the environment.

L4
Definition
Biotic components are all living organisms in an environment, while abiotic components are the non-living physical and chemical factors.
Key Point
Biotic factors reproduce and interact in food webs, whereas abiotic factors like sunlight, water, and temperature set the conditions for life.
Example
In a pond, fish, frogs, and algae are biotic; water, dissolved oxygen, sunlight, and mud are abiotic.
Q15

Describe the major components of the natural environment.

L2
Definition
The natural environment consists of four interacting spheres: lithosphere (land), hydrosphere (water), atmosphere (air), and biosphere (all life).
Key Point
Life thrives in the narrow zone where land, water, and air overlap, and changes in one sphere ripple into the others.
Example
Rain from the atmosphere falls onto lithosphere soil, feeds hydrosphere rivers, and nourishes biosphere forests.
Q16

Discuss any two major environmental challenges facing the world today.

L2
Definition
Two defining global environmental challenges are climate change and biodiversity loss.
Key Point
Rising greenhouse gases drive extreme weather and sea-level rise, while habitat destruction and pollution push species toward extinction and weaken ecosystems.
Example
Record-breaking summer heatwaves across India (climate change) and the bleaching of coral reefs (biodiversity loss).
Q17

Explain how population growth can place pressure on natural resources.

L2
Definition
Rapid population growth increases total demand for food, freshwater, energy, housing land, and waste disposal.
Key Point
When consumption outpaces Earth's regeneration rate, it accelerates deforestation, groundwater depletion, and urban congestion.
Example
Expanding cities converting surrounding farmland and wetlands into housing complexes while over-pumping local aquifers.
Q18

Discuss the importance of environmental awareness in achieving sustainability.

L2
Definition
Environmental awareness is understanding how ecosystems work and how human choices affect environmental health.
Key Point
Informed citizens adopt eco-friendly habits, hold polluters accountable, and support stronger environmental policies.
Example
Public awareness campaigns against single-use plastics have pushed shoppers to carry cloth bags and cities to enforce plastic bans.
Q19

Explain how individual choices can support sustainable development.

L2
Definition
Individual sustainable choices are everyday purchasing, travel, and consumption habits that shrink a person's ecological footprint.
Key Point
When millions of people make small resource-saving decisions, they shift market demand toward cleaner products and lower total emissions.
Example
Choosing public transit or cycling, switching to LED bulbs, buying seasonal local produce, and repairing electronics.
Q20

Suggest practical measures to reduce the environmental impact of everyday activities.

L6
Definition
Practical impact reduction applies the 5 Rs—Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repurpose, and Recycle—across energy, water, food, and transport.
Key Point
Targeting high-impact daily habits like electricity use, food waste, water flow, and commuting delivers the fastest results.
Example
Installing low-flow taps, unplugging idle chargers, segregating wet and dry waste at home, and carpooling to college.

Unit 2 — Ecosystems, Biodiversity and Conservation

CO2 · Q21–Q40
Q21

Define an ecosystem and describe its major components.

L2
Definition
An ecosystem is a functional unit of nature where living organisms interact with one another and with their non-living physical environment.
Key Point
Every ecosystem has two core parts—biotic communities (producers, consumers, decomposers) and abiotic factors (sunlight, water, soil, climate).
Example
A freshwater lake where sunlight and minerals support algae, fish, birds, and bottom-dwelling bacteria.
Q22

Explain the biotic and abiotic components of an ecosystem with examples.

L3
Definition
Biotic components perform biological roles like making food or recycling waste, while abiotic components supply energy, moisture, and nutrients.
Key Point
Removing or altering a key abiotic factor immediately reshapes which biotic species can survive there.
Example
In a forest ecosystem, trees, deer, tigers, and fungi are biotic; rainfall, soil pH, sunlight, and air temperature are abiotic.
Q23

Describe the major functions of an ecosystem.

L2
Definition
Ecosystem functions are the vital natural processes that keep life running: energy flow, nutrient cycling, productivity, and ecological succession.
Key Point
Together, these functions purify air and water, build fertile soil, and keep populations naturally balanced.
Example
In a wetland, plants produce biomass, bacteria recycle nitrogen, and roots filter pollutants from runoff water.
Q24

Explain the flow of energy through an ecosystem.

L2
Definition
Energy flow is the one-way movement of solar energy from the Sun to producers and then up through consumers.
Key Point
Energy is unidirectional and follows the 10% law: only about 10% of energy transfers to the next trophic level, while 90% is lost as heat.
Example
Because of this 90% loss per step, food chains rarely exceed four or five levels, such as grass → rabbit → fox → eagle.
Q25

Define a food chain and illustrate it with a suitable example.

L1
Definition
A food chain is a linear sequence showing who eats whom as energy passes from one organism to the next.
Key Point
Every food chain starts with a producer (autotroph) that captures sunlight and ends with top carnivores and decomposers.
Example
Grass (producer) → Grasshopper (primary consumer) → Frog (secondary consumer) → Snake (tertiary consumer) → Hawk (top predator).
Q26

Define a food web and explain how it differs from a food chain.

L2
Definition
A food web is a network of interconnected food chains showing all the feeding relationships in an ecosystem.
Key Point
Unlike a single fragile food chain, a food web offers alternate food pathways, making the ecosystem far more stable if one species declines.
Example
In a forest, a snake may eat frogs, mice, or birds, while hawks eat both snakes and rabbits—forming an interlocking web.
Q27

Explain the roles of producers, consumers, and decomposers in an ecosystem.

L2
Definition
Producers make food via photosynthesis, consumers eat other organisms for energy, and decomposers break down dead organic matter.
Key Point
Without producers no energy enters the system, and without decomposers nutrients would stay locked in dead bodies instead of returning to soil.
Example
Oak trees (producers), deer and wolves (consumers), and mushrooms and soil bacteria (decomposers).
Q28

Describe the major types of ecosystems with examples.

L3
Definition
Ecosystems are broadly classified into natural terrestrial (land), natural aquatic (water), and artificial (human-made) ecosystems.
Key Point
Each type is shaped by its dominant climate, water salinity, and human management.
Example
Terrestrial: Western Ghats rainforest or Thar Desert; Aquatic: Chilika Lake or coral reefs; Artificial: rice paddy field or aquarium.
Q29

Differentiate between terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems.

L4
Definition
Terrestrial ecosystems exist on land with air as the medium, while aquatic ecosystems exist in freshwater or marine water.
Key Point
Land ecosystems face wider temperature and moisture swings, whereas aquatic ecosystems have steadier temperatures but limited dissolved oxygen and light depth.
Example
A deciduous forest relies on rainfall and deep roots, while a marine coral reef depends on water salinity, currents, and shallow sunlight.
Q30

Define biodiversity and explain its importance.

L2
Definition
Biodiversity is the variety of all life on Earth, spanning genetic diversity, species diversity, and ecosystem diversity.
Key Point
High biodiversity boosts ecosystem resilience, provides food, medicines, and pollination, and buffers nature against disease and climate shocks.
Example
Diverse crop varieties ensure that if one blight hits a single rice strain, other resistant varieties still secure the harvest.
Q31

Explain species biodiversity and its significance.

L2
Definition
Species biodiversity refers to both the number of different species (richness) and how evenly individuals are distributed (evenness) in an area.
Key Point
Each species fills a unique ecological niche; losing keystone species can trigger a domino collapse across the whole community.
Example
Bees pollinate flowering crops while bats control night-flying insect pests—both are essential species in agricultural landscapes.
Q32

Describe the ecological, economic, and social values of biodiversity.

L2
Definition
Biodiversity delivers ecological services (pollination, carbon storage), economic goods (food, timber, drugs), and social/cultural meaning (traditions, ecotourism).
Key Point
Valuing all three dimensions shows that protecting nature supports both GDP and community well-being.
Example
The neem tree provides ecological pest control, commercial medicinal oils, and deep cultural heritage across Indian households.
Q33

Discuss the major threats to biodiversity.

L2
Definition
The five major threats to biodiversity are summarized by HIPPO: Habitat loss, Invasive species, Pollution, Population pressure/overexploitation, and Climate change.
Key Point
Habitat destruction is the single biggest driver today, often amplified when invasive species or warming climates hit already stressed populations.
Example
Clearing tropical forests for palm oil plantations while water hyacinth chokes local freshwater lakes.
Q34

Explain how habitat loss and fragmentation affect biodiversity.

L2
Definition
Habitat loss destroys an organism's home completely, while fragmentation splits one large habitat into small, isolated patches.
Key Point
Isolated patches trap small populations, reduce genetic diversity through inbreeding, and increase dangerous edge effects and roadkills.
Example
A highway cutting through a tiger reserve separates breeding pairs and forces wildlife into conflict with nearby villages.
Q35

Define in-situ conservation and give suitable examples.

L1
Definition
In-situ conservation means protecting species right inside their natural habitats and ecosystems.
Key Point
It preserves not just one species, but its entire food web, evolutionary process, and natural home.
Example
National parks (Jim Corbett), wildlife sanctuaries (Periyar), biosphere reserves (Nilgiri), and sacred groves.
Q36

Define ex-situ conservation and give suitable examples.

L1
Definition
Ex-situ conservation means protecting threatened species outside their natural habitats in controlled human-managed facilities.
Key Point
It acts as an emergency backup ark for critically endangered species whose wild habitats are destroyed or unsafe.
Example
Botanical gardens, zoological parks, seed banks (like Svalbard Global Seed Vault), and gene/cryopreservation banks.
Q37

Differentiate between in-situ and ex-situ conservation.

L4
Definition
In-situ protects species on-site in the wild, whereas ex-situ protects them off-site in specialized facilities.
Key Point
In-situ allows natural evolution and large populations at lower cost per species; ex-situ provides intensive medical care and breeding for tiny, endangered populations.
Example
Protecting Asiatic lions in Gir National Park is in-situ; breeding endangered gharials in a captive zoo program is ex-situ.
Q38

Explain the role of protected areas in biodiversity conservation.

L2
Definition
Protected areas are legally designated zones—such as national parks, sanctuaries, and biosphere reserves—managed primarily to conserve nature.
Key Point
They restrict poaching, logging, and encroachment, provide safe breeding corridors, and serve as living laboratories for ecological research.
Example
Project Tiger reserves across India helped tiger numbers recover by securing core forest habitats and buffer zones.
Q39

Describe the role of botanical gardens, zoos, and seed banks in conservation.

L2
Definition
Botanical gardens preserve living plants, zoos support captive breeding and education, and seed banks freeze crop and wild plant seeds for long-term storage.
Key Point
Together they safeguard genetic diversity, enable reintroduction into restored habitats, and educate the public on extinction risks.
Example
India's National Bureau of Plant Genetic Resources (NBPGR) stores hundreds of thousands of seed samples to protect future food security.
Q40

Describe a case study of ecosystem restoration and explain its key lessons.

L4
Definition
Ecosystem restoration is actively assisting the recovery of degraded, damaged, or destroyed habitats.
Key Point
Key lessons from successful restorations are to use native species, involve local communities, and address root causes like erosion or overgrazing.
Example
The Loess Plateau restoration in China—or the Aravali Biodiversity Park in Gurugram—turned barren, eroded land back into thriving native forests by combining terracing, native planting, and community stewardship.

Unit 3 — Pollution of Air, Water and Soil

CO3 · Q41–Q60
Q41

Define air pollution, water pollution, and soil pollution.

L1
Definition
Air pollution is the contamination of the atmosphere by harmful gases or particles; water pollution is the degradation of water bodies by waste or chemicals; soil pollution is the buildup of toxic substances in land.
Key Point
In all three cases, contaminants exceed nature's self-cleaning capacity and endanger human health and ecosystems.
Example
City smog (air), untreated sewage in rivers (water), and heavy-metal leachate under a landfill (soil).
Q42

List and explain the major sources of air pollution.

L2
Definition
Air pollution comes from natural sources (volcanoes, wildfires, dust storms) and anthropogenic or human-made sources (vehicles, power plants, factories, crop burning).
Key Point
Human combustion of fossil fuels is the dominant controllable source of harmful particulate matter (PM2.5/PM10), SO₂, NOₓ, and CO.
Example
Coal-fired thermal power stations emitting sulfur dioxide and diesel trucks releasing fine soot particles in metro cities.
Q43

Discuss the effects of air pollution on human health.

L2
Definition
Air pollution harms the respiratory, cardiovascular, and nervous systems, causing both short-term irritation and chronic disease.
Key Point
Fine particles (PM2.5) penetrate deep into the lungs and bloodstream, triggering asthma, bronchitis, heart disease, strokes, and premature death.
Example
During winter smog spikes in Delhi-NCR, hospital visits for childhood asthma and breathing distress rise sharply.
Q44

Explain the effects of air pollution on plants, animals, and ecosystems.

L2
Definition
Air pollutants damage plant leaves, acidify soil and lakes, and poison wildlife through direct inhalation or contaminated food.
Key Point
Acid rain (from SO₂ and NOₓ) strips nutrients from forest soils and kills fish in acidified lakes, while ground-level ozone cuts crop yields.
Example
Acid rain damaging conifer forests in Europe and corroding marble monuments like the Taj Mahal.
Q45

Describe methods for preventing and controlling air pollution.

L2
Definition
Air pollution control combines source prevention (clean fuels, renewables) with end-of-pipe technologies (filters, scrubbers, catalytic converters).
Key Point
Preventing emissions at the source is always cheaper and cleaner than trapping pollutants after burning fuel.
Example
Installing electrostatic precipitators in factory chimneys, switching buses to electric or CNG, and expanding urban green belts.
Q46

Explain the role of vehicles and industries in urban air pollution.

L2
Definition
Vehicles are mobile emission sources concentrated at breathing height, while industries are stationary point sources releasing high volumes of smoke and gases.
Key Point
Together they produce nitrogen oxides, hydrocarbons, and particulates that react in sunlight to form dense photochemical smog.
Example
Rush-hour traffic jams combined with nearby brick kilns and manufacturing estates creating haze over industrial corridors.
Q47

Define water pollution and describe its major sources.

L2
Definition
Water pollution is any physical, chemical, or biological change that makes water unfit for drinking, farming, or aquatic life.
Key Point
Sources are either point sources (identifiable pipes like factory outlets) or non-point sources (diffuse runoff from farms and city streets).
Example
Untreated municipal sewage, textile dye effluents, oil spills, and fertilizer runoff washing into rivers.
Q48

Discuss the effects of water pollution on human health and aquatic life.

L2
Definition
Polluted water spreads infectious waterborne diseases in humans and suffocates aquatic life through toxicity and oxygen depletion.
Key Point
Excess nutrients cause eutrophication (algal blooms) that consume dissolved oxygen, creating dead zones where fish cannot survive.
Example
Pathogens cause cholera and typhoid in humans, while mercury pollution caused Minamata disease and massive fish kills.
Q49

Explain the physical, chemical, and biological indicators of water pollution.

L2
Definition
Water quality is measured using physical indicators (turbidity, odor, temperature), chemical indicators (pH, Dissolved Oxygen, BOD, COD, heavy metals), and biological indicators (coliform bacteria, indicator species).
Key Point
High Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) and low Dissolved Oxygen (DO) immediately signal heavy organic sewage pollution.
Example
Finding E. coli coliform bacteria proves fecal contamination, while low DO below 4 mg/L warns that fish are suffocating.
Q50

Describe methods used to prevent and control water pollution.

L2
Definition
Water pollution control relies on treating wastewater before discharge, curbing agricultural runoff, enforcing laws, and conserving water.
Key Point
Strict industrial Effluent Treatment Plants (ETPs) and zero-liquid-discharge systems stop toxins before they ever reach rivers.
Example
Using drip irrigation to cut fertilizer runoff, banning direct sewage dumping, and installing community sewage treatment plants.
Q51

Explain the importance of sewage treatment in pollution control.

L2
Definition
Sewage treatment removes solids, organic waste, and pathogens from domestic wastewater through primary (physical), secondary (biological), and tertiary (chemical/disinfection) stages.
Key Point
It prevents river eutrophication, blocks waterborne epidemics, and allows treated greywater to be safely reused for gardening or cooling.
Example
A municipal Sewage Treatment Plant (STP) using aeration tanks and UV disinfection to turn city wastewater into safe irrigation water.
Q52

Define soil contamination and discuss its major sources.

L2
Definition
Soil contamination is the presence of toxic chemicals, salts, or waste in soil at concentrations harmful to plants, microbes, or humans.
Key Point
Major sources include excessive agrochemicals, industrial waste dumping, leaking underground tanks, mining tailings, and unlined landfills.
Example
Heavy metals like lead and chromium seeping into soil around poorly managed electroplating factories or e-waste yards.
Q53

Explain how pesticides and fertilizers can contaminate soil.

L2
Definition
Overusing chemical fertilizers alters soil pH and salinity, while persistent pesticides kill beneficial soil microbes and accumulate in topsoil.
Key Point
Excess nitrates also leach down into groundwater, and persistent chemicals biomagnify as they move up the food chain.
Example
Repeated heavy spraying of organochlorine pesticides like DDT left long-lasting residues in farmland soils and bird eggs.
Q54

Discuss the effects of soil contamination on agriculture and human health.

L2
Definition
Contaminated soil reduces crop fertility and yield, kills earthworms, and transfers toxins into human food and drinking water.
Key Point
Humans absorb soil pollutants through contaminated vegetables, dust inhalation, or polluted well water, raising risks of organ damage and cancer.
Example
Cadmium-contaminated paddy soils in Japan caused painful Itai-Itai bone disease in people who ate the locally grown rice.
Q55

Describe suitable remediation methods for contaminated soil.

L2
Definition
Soil remediation cleans polluted land using biological methods (bioremediation, phytoremediation), chemical treatments (soil washing), or physical methods (excavation, thermal desorption).
Key Point
Bioremediation and phytoremediation are eco-friendly and cost-effective because living microbes and plants naturally break down or absorb toxins.
Example
Planting sunflowers or Indian mustard (phytoremediation) to extract heavy metals from contaminated industrial plots.
Q56

Explain the difference between pollution prevention and pollution remediation.

L2
Definition
Pollution prevention stops waste and toxins from being created in the first place; pollution remediation cleans up damage after contamination has already happened.
Key Point
Prevention is proactive, cheaper, and protects health immediately, whereas remediation is reactive, expensive, and often takes decades.
Example
Switching a factory to non-toxic water-based dyes is prevention; excavating and treating dye-soaked soil years later is remediation.
Q57

Discuss a case study of water pollution and the remedial measures used.

L4
Definition
The Ganga River pollution crisis illustrates severe domestic sewage and industrial tannery discharge degrading a major river basin.
Key Point
Remedial action under the Namami Gange programme focuses on expanding STPs, relocating or regulating tanneries, riverfront cleaning, and real-time water monitoring.
Example
Installing high-capacity sewage treatment plants in Kanpur and Varanasi and enforcing strict Effluent Treatment Plants on leather tanneries.
Q58

Discuss a case study of air pollution and the actions taken to address it.

L4
Definition
Beijing's and Delhi's severe urban smog crises highlight the combined impact of coal power, traffic, construction dust, and seasonal biomass burning.
Key Point
Targeted multi-sector action—tightening fuel standards, shifting to electric/CNG transit, shutting old coal plants, and enforcing graded response plans—drives measurable improvement.
Example
Delhi's transition of public buses and autos to CNG and BS-VI fuel standards alongside the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP).
Q59

Discuss a case study of soil pollution and the actions taken to address it.

L4
Definition
The Love Canal disaster in New York occurred when a neighborhood and school were built over a buried chemical waste dump.
Key Point
After toxic chemicals seeped into basements and harmed residents' health, the site was evacuated, capped, remediated, and sparked the US Superfund cleanup law.
Example
Love Canal proved why strict hazardous-waste containment, site testing, and 'polluter pays' laws are essential before urban development.
Q60

Suggest an integrated plan to reduce air, water, and soil pollution in a town.

L6
Definition
An integrated town pollution plan tackles air, water, and soil together because pollutants move easily between all three mediums.
Key Point
Combine clean public transit and green belts (air), 100% sewage treatment and rainwater harvesting (water), and waste segregation with composting and sanitary landfills (soil).
Example
Indore's model—door-to-door waste segregation, bio-CNG plants from wet waste, mechanized street sweeping, and STP reuse—demonstrates integrated urban cleanliness.

Unit 4 — Natural Resources, Energy and Climate Change

CO4 · Q61–Q80
Q61

Define renewable and non-renewable resources with examples.

L1
Definition
Renewable resources replenish naturally on a human timescale, whereas non-renewable resources exist in finite stocks that take millions of years to form.
Key Point
Even renewable resources like forests or groundwater can run dry if we harvest them faster than nature regenerates them.
Example
Renewable: sunlight, wind, flowing water, forests; Non-renewable: coal, crude oil, natural gas, uranium, and iron ore.
Q62

Differentiate between renewable and non-renewable energy resources.

L4
Definition
Renewable energy comes from continuously replenished natural flows with low operational emissions; non-renewable energy comes from exhaustible fuels with high carbon emissions.
Key Point
Renewables offer energy security and clean air but can be intermittent; fossil fuels provide steady baseload power but drive climate change and price volatility.
Example
Solar photovoltaic parks generate zero tailpipe CO₂, whereas coal power stations deplete finite mines and emit heavy greenhouse gases.
Q63

Explain the advantages and limitations of solar energy.

L2
Definition
Solar energy converts sunlight into electricity (via PV panels) or heat (via solar thermal collectors).
Key Point
Advantages: abundant, clean, silent, and modular for rooftops; Limitations: intermittent at night or cloudy days, needs battery storage, and requires land area for utility scale.
Example
India's Bhadla Solar Park in Rajasthan generates gigawatts of cheap clean electricity using abundant desert sunlight.
Q64

Describe the uses and benefits of wind energy.

L2
Definition
Wind energy uses moving air to spin turbine blades connected to an electrical generator.
Key Point
It produces zero emissions during operation, uses minimal ground footprint so farming can continue underneath, and has low running costs.
Example
Wind farms across Tamil Nadu and Gujarat supply clean grid electricity while farmers continue grazing livestock around the turbine bases.
Q65

Explain the environmental impacts of fossil fuel consumption.

L2
Definition
Burning coal, oil, and natural gas releases massive CO₂, sulfur and nitrogen oxides, heavy metals, and soot.
Key Point
Beyond driving global warming, extracting and burning fossil fuels causes habitat destruction from mining, oil spills, acid rain, and severe urban air pollution.
Example
Open-cast coal mining clears forests and pollutes nearby streams, while burning that coal fuels both smog and climate warming.
Q66

Define sustainable natural resources management.

L1
Definition
Sustainable natural resources management is the planned use, conservation, and regeneration of land, water, forests, and minerals so they last for future generations.
Key Point
It balances ecological limits with human livelihoods through science-based quotas, reuse, and community governance.
Example
Watershed management programs that recharge groundwater while regulating borewell pumping for local farmers.
Q67

Describe practical methods for managing water resources sustainably.

L3
Definition
Sustainable water management focuses on catching rain, cutting waste, recycling greywater, and protecting watersheds.
Key Point
Since agriculture uses the largest share of freshwater, precision irrigation and rainwater recharge deliver the biggest water savings.
Example
Drip irrigation on farms, rooftop rainwater harvesting in apartments, fixing leaky city pipes, and reviving local check dams.
Q68

Explain how forests and biodiversity can be managed sustainably.

L2
Definition
Sustainable forest management harvests timber and forest products only within regrowth limits while protecting wildlife habitats and soil.
Key Point
Key tools include selective logging instead of clear-cutting, reforestation with native trees, forest fire control, and Joint Forest Management with local tribes.
Example
FSC-certified sustainable forestry and community-managed bamboo groves that provide steady rural income without destroying canopy cover.
Q69

Discuss strategies for reducing energy consumption and improving energy efficiency.

L3
Definition
Energy conservation means using less energy by changing habits, while energy efficiency means doing the same work with less energy using better technology.
Key Point
The cleanest, cheapest kilowatt-hour is the one you never need to generate.
Example
Switching to 5-star BEE-rated inverter ACs and LED lights, insulating buildings, conducting industrial energy audits, and using smart thermostats.
Q70

Define global warming and climate change, and distinguish between them.

L4
Definition
Global warming is the long-term rise in Earth's average surface temperature; climate change is the broader shift in weather patterns, rainfall, storms, and sea levels caused by that warming.
Key Point
Global warming is the primary driver (the fever), while climate change is the full set of planetary symptoms.
Example
A 1.2°C rise in average global temperature is global warming; erratic monsoons, melting glaciers, and stronger cyclones are climate change.
Q71

Explain the major causes of climate change.

L2
Definition
Modern climate change is primarily driven by human-emitted greenhouse gases—CO₂, methane (CH₄), nitrous oxide (N₂O), and fluorinated gases.
Key Point
Burning fossil fuels for power and transport, deforestation (which removes carbon sinks), intensive livestock farming, and industrial cement production are the main sources.
Example
Coal power plants release CO₂ while clearing the Amazon rainforest both emits stored carbon and reduces future carbon absorption.
Q72

Discuss the environmental effects of climate change.

L2
Definition
Climate change reshapes physical ecosystems through melting glaciers, rising seas, ocean acidification, droughts, wildfires, and extreme floods.
Key Point
Warmer oceans fuel stronger tropical cyclones and absorb excess CO₂, turning seawater more acidic and harming shell-forming marine life.
Example
Retreating Himalayan glaciers threaten long-term river flows, while rising seas erode low-lying islands and coastal Sundarbans deltas.
Q73

Explain the effects of climate change on human health.

L2
Definition
Climate change threatens human health through deadly heatwaves, worse air pollution, spreading vector-borne diseases, and food and water insecurity.
Key Point
Vulnerable groups—outdoor workers, children, and the elderly—face the highest risks from heatstroke and climate-linked malnutrition.
Example
Warmer, wetter conditions expand the range of mosquitoes, increasing outbreaks of dengue and malaria in previously cooler regions.
Q74

Describe how climate change affects plants, animals, and natural habitats.

L2
Definition
Warming temperatures and shifting rainfall force species to migrate poleward or uphill, disrupt flowering and breeding seasons, and degrade habitats.
Key Point
Species that cannot move fast enough—like coral reefs or alpine wildlife—face severe population crashes and local extinction.
Example
Marine heatwaves trigger mass coral bleaching on the Great Barrier Reef, stripping shelter from thousands of reef fish species.
Q75

Differentiate between climate change mitigation and adaptation.

L4
Definition
Mitigation tackles the root cause by reducing or capturing greenhouse gas emissions; adaptation adjusts human and natural systems to cope with climate impacts already underway.
Key Point
We need both: mitigation limits how bad climate change gets, while adaptation protects people from the changes already locked in.
Example
Replacing coal plants with solar power is mitigation; building coastal cyclone shelters and drought-tolerant crops is adaptation.
Q76

Give examples of mitigation strategies for climate change.

L6
Definition
Mitigation strategies cut emissions across energy, transport, industry, buildings, and land use while expanding carbon sinks.
Key Point
Decarbonizing electricity and electrifying transport deliver the largest rapid cuts in carbon pollution.
Example
Scaling solar and wind grids, adopting electric vehicles, restoring mangrove forests, cutting methane leaks, and improving building insulation.
Q77

Give examples of adaptation strategies for climate change.

L6
Definition
Adaptation strategies build resilience against heatwaves, floods, droughts, and rising seas.
Key Point
Effective adaptation combines hard engineering (flood barriers) with nature-based solutions (wetlands) and early warning systems.
Example
Developing drought-resistant millet varieties, painting urban roofs white to cool cities, restoring coastal mangroves, and setting up heat-action alerts.
Q78

Explain the main purpose and significance of the Kyoto Protocol.

L2
Definition
Adopted in 1997 under the UNFCCC, the Kyoto Protocol was the first legally binding international treaty requiring developed nations to cut greenhouse gas emissions.
Key Point
It introduced 'common but differentiated responsibilities' and market mechanisms like carbon trading and the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM).
Example
Under the CDM, developed countries funded clean wind and biogas projects in developing nations like India to earn certified emission credits.
Q79

Describe the main objectives of the Paris Agreement.

L2
Definition
Adopted in 2015, the Paris Agreement unites nearly all nations to limit global warming well below 2°C—and pursue 1.5°C—above pre-industrial levels.
Key Point
Unlike Kyoto, every country submits voluntary national climate plans called Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), reviewed and strengthened every five years.
Example
India's Paris NDC pledges to expand non-fossil electricity capacity and reduce the emissions intensity of its GDP.
Q80

Analyse the impacts of climate change on communities and suggest sustainable adaptation measures.

L4
Definition
Climate change hits coastal, farming, and low-income urban communities hardest through crop failure, water scarcity, flooding, and lost livelihoods.
Key Point
Sustainable adaptation empowers local communities with resilient agriculture, decentralized water storage, climate-proof housing, and early warnings.
Example
In coastal Odisha, community cyclone shelters, mangrove restoration, and salt-tolerant rice varieties dramatically cut casualties and crop losses.

Unit 5 — Sustainable Consumption, Green Technology and Sustainable Urban Planning

CO5 · Q81–Q100
Q81

Explain how a minimalist lifestyle can promote sustainable consumption in urban environments.

L2
Definition
Minimalism is intentionally owning and buying fewer, higher-quality items that serve real needs.
Key Point
In high-consumption cities, minimalism directly cuts raw material extraction, manufacturing emissions, packaging waste, and clutter.
Example
Building a small capsule wardrobe of durable cotton clothes instead of buying disposable fast fashion every month.
Q82

Suggest practical ways individuals can reduce waste and resource use in daily life.

L3
Definition
Daily waste reduction focuses on preventing single-use trash, conserving utilities, and extending product lifespans.
Key Point
Small habits repeated 365 days a year save thousands of liters of water and hundreds of kilograms of landfill waste per household.
Example
Carrying a reusable bottle and steel lunchbox, composting kitchen scraps, printing double-sided, and donating or repairing old gadgets.
Q83

Explain the principles of sustainable consumption and production.

L2
Definition
Sustainable Consumption and Production (SDG 12) means doing more and better with less—cutting resource use and pollution across a product's entire lifecycle.
Key Point
Producers design durable, repairable, low-waste goods while consumers choose eco-labeled products and minimize waste.
Example
Modular smartphones designed for easy battery replacement paired with manufacturer take-back recycling programs.
Q84

Define green technology and describe its role in sustainable development.

L2
Definition
Green technology (clean tech) is the application of science and engineering to create products and processes that conserve resources and minimize environmental harm.
Key Point
It decouples economic growth from pollution by making clean energy, clean water, and low-waste manufacturing affordable at scale.
Example
Solar photovoltaics, electric vehicles, LED lighting, biodegradable packaging, and membrane wastewater recycling.
Q85

Design an energy-efficient home using green technology and justify your choices.

L6
Definition
An energy-efficient green home integrates passive cooling, rooftop solar, efficient appliances, water recycling, and low-carbon materials.
Key Point
Combining passive design (lowering demand first) with clean generation (solar) can cut a home's net energy bill by 60–80%.
Example
A home with cross-ventilation, double-glazed windows, rooftop solar PV + solar water heater, 5-star inverter appliances, LEDs, and rainwater harvesting.
Q86

Explain how passive solar design can reduce energy consumption in buildings.

L6
Definition
Passive solar design uses a building's orientation, windows, shading, insulation, and thermal mass to naturally heat or cool interiors without mechanical equipment.
Key Point
It harvests winter sunlight while blocking harsh summer sun, slashing air-conditioning and heating loads for decades at near-zero operating cost.
Example
Orienting living spaces to catch breezes, adding deep sun-shades (chhajjas) over south/west windows, and using insulated walls.
Q87

Discuss the benefits of energy-efficient lighting and appliances.

L2
Definition
Energy-efficient lighting (LEDs) and star-rated appliances deliver the same light or cooling using a fraction of the electricity.
Key Point
They cut household electricity bills immediately, last much longer than older models, and reduce peak load on coal power plants.
Example
Replacing a 60W incandescent bulb with a 9W LED cuts lighting electricity use by roughly 85% and lasts over 10 times longer.
Q88

Explain the importance of sustainable building materials.

L2
Definition
Sustainable building materials are locally sourced, renewable, recycled, or low-embodied-energy materials that last long and release no indoor toxins.
Key Point
Construction cement and steel account for massive global CO₂; greener alternatives shrink a building's carbon footprint before anyone even moves in.
Example
Fly-ash bricks (reusing power-plant waste), bamboo flooring, compressed stabilized earth blocks, and recycled steel.
Q89

Describe how rainwater harvesting can support sustainable housing.

L2
Definition
Rainwater harvesting collects rooftop or surface rainwater, filters it, and stores it in tanks or channels it into groundwater recharge pits.
Key Point
It reduces dependence on municipal water and tankers, cuts urban monsoon flooding, and replenishes falling urban water tables.
Example
A housing society in Pune routing roof downpipes through sand-gravel filters into a borewell recharge pit and underground storage sump.
Q90

Explain how rooftop solar panels can contribute to a green home.

L2
Definition
Rooftop solar panels convert unused roof space into a clean, decentralized power plant for the household.
Key Point
Through net metering, excess daytime power is exported to the grid, slashing monthly bills and offsetting tonnes of CO₂ over a 25-year lifespan.
Example
A 3 kW residential rooftop solar array generating roughly 12–15 units per day—enough to power most daily home appliances.
Q91

Explain how agroecological farming can improve food security and reduce environmental impact.

L2
Definition
Agroecology applies ecological principles to farming—working with natural biodiversity, soil biology, and local knowledge rather than heavy synthetic chemicals.
Key Point
It builds healthy, drought-resilient soils, diversifies farmer harvests for stable food security, and prevents fertilizer and pesticide runoff.
Example
Intercropping legumes with millets naturally fixes nitrogen in soil, cuts pest outbreaks, and gives farmers two reliable food crops.
Q92

Describe sustainable agricultural practices with suitable examples.

L3
Definition
Sustainable agriculture produces healthy food while preserving soil fertility, water, and rural ecosystems.
Key Point
Core methods include crop rotation, organic composting, drip irrigation, integrated pest management (IPM), and agroforestry.
Example
Growing neem-border trees for natural pest control, rotating wheat with pulses to restore soil nitrogen, and using vermicompost.
Q93

Suggest a project combining sustainable agriculture and urban planning, such as rooftop farming.

L6
Definition
A municipal rooftop-farming initiative converts flat apartment, school, and mall roofs into productive community vegetable gardens.
Key Point
It cools buildings beneath (cutting AC use), absorbs stormwater, turns kitchen compost into local food, and slashes 'food miles' from distant farms.
Example
A college campus rooftop hydroponic and raised-bed farm watered with treated greywater that supplies fresh greens to the hostel canteen.
Q94

Explain how urban farming can improve urban sustainability and resilience.

L2
Definition
Urban farming grows food inside cities using rooftops, balconies, vertical racks, and vacant plots.
Key Point
It strengthens local food security during supply disruptions, cools urban heat islands, recycles organic city waste, and builds community bonds.
Example
Community allotment gardens and vertical hydroponic farms in cities like Bengaluru and Singapore supplying fresh herbs year-round.
Q95

Develop a plan for introducing a bicycle-sharing system into a city's transport network.

L6
Definition
A city bicycle-sharing plan integrates docking stations at metro/bus hubs, dedicated safe bike lanes, app-based rentals, and affordable pricing.
Key Point
Safety and first/last-mile connectivity to public transit—not just buying bikes—determine whether commuters actually ride daily.
Example
Placing smart bike docks outside Pune Metro stations and college gates, linked to a single transit card with protected painted lanes.
Q96

Explain how bicycle-sharing and active transport can reduce carbon emissions.

L2
Definition
Active transport—walking and cycling—replaces short car and motorbike trips with zero-emission human-powered travel.
Key Point
Because a huge share of urban trips are under 5 km, shifting them to bikes cuts tailpipe CO₂, traffic jams, noise, and fuel imports.
Example
A commuter swapping a 4 km daily solo car ride for a shared bicycle avoids hundreds of kilograms of CO₂ emissions each year.
Q97

Discuss the role of public transport and walkable neighbourhoods in sustainable urban planning.

L2
Definition
Transit-oriented, walkable neighborhoods place homes, shops, schools, and transit stops within easy walking distance.
Key Point
One full bus or metro train replaces dozens of private cars, cutting per-person emissions, road space needed, and urban air pollution.
Example
Cities with shaded footpaths, safe crossings, and frequent metro-feeder buses allow residents to live comfortably without owning a car.
Q98

Explain how waste segregation, reuse, and recycling support a circular economy.

L2
Definition
A circular economy eliminates waste by keeping materials in continuous use—through segregation at source, reuse, repair, composting, and recycling—rather than 'take-make-dispose'.
Key Point
Clean segregation into wet, dry, and hazardous bins is the essential first step; mixed garbage destroys recyclable value and clogs landfills.
Example
Composting wet kitchen waste into fertilizer while recycling clean paper, glass, and PET plastic back into new packaging.
Q99

Suggest measures a city can take to reduce its ecological footprint.

L6
Definition
A city's ecological footprint shrinks when it shifts to clean energy, compact transit-friendly growth, circular waste systems, and urban greening.
Key Point
Coordinated policies across buildings, transport, water, and waste cut both local pollution and global resource demand.
Example
Mandating green building codes, electrifying municipal buses, protecting urban lakes, composting 100% of organic waste, and expanding tree canopies.
Q100

Prepare an integrated plan for a sustainable neighbourhood using green buildings, urban farming, and sustainable transport.

L6
Definition
A sustainable neighborhood weaves together passive-solar green buildings, decentralized water/solar utilities, community rooftop farms, and car-light walkable streets.
Key Point
Integrating all systems on one site creates synergies: compost feeds urban farms, greywater irrigates parks, and shaded walkways connect homes to transit.
Example
A 500-home eco-township featuring solar microgrids, rainwater recharge parks, community vegetable plots, protected cycle tracks, and a zero-waste composting hub.

Unit 6 — Corporate Sustainability, CSR, Environmental Activism and NGOs

CO6 · Q101–Q120
Q101

Define corporate sustainability and explain its importance in business operations.

L2
Definition
Corporate sustainability is managing a company's operations to create long-term value while protecting the environment and supporting society (the ESG framework).
Key Point
It matters because businesses control huge resource and emission footprints—and face rising regulatory, climate, and reputational risks if they ignore sustainability.
Example
An IT campus running on 100% renewable electricity and zero-landfill waste management across its offices.
Q102

Explain the relationship between corporate sustainability and long-term business success.

L2
Definition
Sustainable companies lower operating costs, attract loyal customers and talent, avoid regulatory fines, and secure cheaper green financing.
Key Point
Far from hurting profits, sustainability builds resilience against energy price spikes, resource shortages, and shifting consumer expectations.
Example
Companies that cut packaging weight and switch to solar power save millions in energy and logistics costs while strengthening brand trust.
Q103

Define Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) and explain its main objectives.

L2
Definition
Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) is a business model where companies voluntarily—or by law—contribute to social welfare and environmental protection beyond making profits.
Key Point
Its core objectives are ethical governance, community upliftment, environmental stewardship, and transparent accountability to stakeholders.
Example
Under India's Companies Act (2013), eligible firms spend at least 2% of average net profits on CSR areas like clean water, education, and afforestation.
Q104

Analyse how CSR initiatives can make businesses more sustainable.

L4
Definition
Strategic CSR embeds social and environmental goals directly into a firm's supply chain, workforce, and local operating communities.
Key Point
When CSR solves real environmental risks—like watershed restoration near a beverage plant—it protects both local villagers and the company's long-term operations.
Example
A manufacturing firm funding local watershed recharge and skill-training centers earns a strong social license to operate.
Q105

Discuss the long-term benefits of CSR for society and the economy with an example.

L2
Definition
CSR channels private capital and management expertise into public needs like clean energy, healthcare, education, and ecosystem restoration.
Key Point
Over time, healthier, better-educated communities and restored natural resources strengthen the entire regional economy.
Example
ITC's e-Choupal and social forestry CSR programs improved rural farmer incomes while expanding sustainable tree cover across thousands of hectares.
Q106

Describe examples of environmental responsibility in business operations.

L2
Definition
Environmental responsibility in business means actively minimizing pollution, conserving water and energy, and designing eco-friendly products.
Key Point
It covers daily operations—from green factories and paperless offices to recyclable packaging and safe hazardous-waste disposal.
Example
Tata Power expanding solar/wind generation, or retail brands switching from plastic wrap to recycled cardboard packaging.
Q107

Explain how businesses can reduce energy use, waste, and emissions.

L2
Definition
Businesses cut their footprint by running energy audits, switching to renewables, adopting lean/circular manufacturing, and electrifying delivery fleets.
Key Point
Measuring emissions across Scope 1, 2, and 3 identifies the biggest waste hotspots for immediate savings.
Example
A factory installing waste-heat recovery boilers, reusing treated process water, and shifting regional deliveries to electric vans.
Q108

Discuss the role of ethical sourcing and sustainable supply chains in corporate sustainability.

L2
Definition
Ethical sourcing ensures raw materials are obtained without deforestation, pollution, or labor exploitation across every supplier tier.
Key Point
Because most of a company's environmental impact lies in its supply chain (Scope 3), auditing suppliers is crucial for genuine sustainability.
Example
A coffee or chocolate brand sourcing only Fairtrade and Rainforest Alliance-certified beans grown without clearing native forests.
Q109

Explain the main ideas behind environmental activism.

L2
Definition
Environmental activism is organized collective action by citizens to protect ecosystems, oppose destructive projects, and demand stronger environmental laws.
Key Point
It rests on environmental justice, peaceful advocacy, public awareness, and holding governments and corporations accountable.
Example
The historic Chipko Movement in Uttarakhand, where villagers hugged trees to stop commercial logging in Himalayan forests.
Q110

Describe how environmental activism influences global sustainability efforts.

L2
Definition
Activism shifts public opinion, pushes climate and conservation onto political agendas, and pressures companies to abandon harmful practices.
Key Point
From local tree-saving campaigns to global youth climate marches, public pressure has accelerated renewable targets and plastic bans worldwide.
Example
Global youth climate strikes and grassroots campaigns helped push governments to strengthen net-zero pledges and divest from coal.
Q111

Suggest ways individuals can participate in environmental activism.

L6
Definition
Individuals can join activism through local cleanups, tree-planting drives, signing petitions, attending public hearings, and eco-volunteering.
Key Point
Consistent local action—backed by accurate science and constructive solutions—creates far more impact than one-off protests.
Example
Joining a weekend river cleanup drive, writing to municipal representatives for safe cycle lanes, or starting a zero-waste club on campus.
Q112

Discuss the challenges faced by environmental activists and suggest ways to overcome them.

L6
Definition
Activists often face funding shortages, public apathy, misinformation, bureaucratic delays, and even legal or physical intimidation.
Key Point
Overcoming these barriers requires building broad community coalitions, using verified scientific data, legal aid networks, and constructive media outreach.
Example
Partnering citizen groups with university researchers and environmental lawyers to file evidence-based Public Interest Litigations (PILs).
Q113

Explain how local communities can contribute to environmental protection.

L2
Definition
Local communities protect the environment through traditional ecological knowledge, collective resource rules, lake cleanups, and neighborhood waste management.
Key Point
Because residents live closest to local forests, lakes, and wells, they notice degradation first and have the strongest stake in long-term care.
Example
Village water committees in Maharashtra building check dams and agreeing on shared groundwater rules to beat drought.
Q114

Evaluate examples of successful community-led sustainability actions.

L5
Definition
Successful community-led projects prove that grassroots ownership delivers lasting results where top-down schemes often fail.
Key Point
Strong local leadership, fair benefit-sharing, and transparent monitoring are the common ingredients of enduring community success.
Example
Ralegan Siddhi and Hiware Bazar in Maharashtra transformed drought-prone villages into water-secure, prosperous communities through watershed conservation and tree planting.
Q115

Define non-governmental organizations (NGOs) and explain their role in environmental protection.

L2
Definition
Non-governmental organizations (NGOs) are independent, non-profit groups formed by citizens to address public issues like conservation and social justice.
Key Point
Environmental NGOs bridge the gap between government policy and ground reality through field projects, independent research, and watchdog monitoring.
Example
Centre for Science and Environment (CSE), WWF-India, and Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS) working on air quality, wildlife, and policy.
Q116

Describe how NGOs contribute to conservation, awareness, and environmental policy.

L2
Definition
NGOs run habitat-restoration projects, publish accessible environmental reports and school programs, and advise lawmakers on scientific standards.
Key Point
Their independence lets them spotlight pollution data, litigate violations, and train local communities in sustainable livelihoods.
Example
WWF-India running wildlife conservation corridors while CSE publishes air-pollution studies that inform national clean-air policy.
Q117

Explain the importance of public participation in environmental decision-making.

L2
Definition
Public participation involves affected citizens in reviewing development projects—such as through Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) public hearings.
Key Point
It surfaces local ecological risks early, prevents unfair displacement, improves project design, and builds public trust in outcomes.
Example
Local fishing communities speaking at a coastal EIA hearing to ensure a new port does not destroy breeding mangroves.
Q118

Compare the roles of individuals, communities, businesses, and NGOs in sustainability.

L4
Definition
Each actor plays a distinct, complementary role: individuals shift daily demand, communities manage shared local resources, businesses innovate and cut industrial footprints, and NGOs research, advocate, and monitor.
Key Point
No single group can solve global sustainability alone; real progress happens when all four reinforce each other alongside strong government policy.
Example
Individuals segregate waste, communities run local composting, businesses design recyclable packaging, and NGOs audit landfill diversion rates.
Q119

Develop a community campaign to reduce plastic waste and explain how its success could be measured.

L6
Definition
A 'Plastic-Free Neighborhood' campaign combines awareness workshops, cloth-bag exchanges with local vendors, refill stations, and weekly zero-waste drives.
Key Point
Success must be measured with concrete KPIs: kg of plastic waste collected, percentage of shops stopping single-use bags, household participation rate, and repeat audits over 6 months.
Example
Tracking a 60% drop in single-use plastic bags at the local vegetable market within 90 days through monthly vendor surveys and waste-bin audits.
Q120

Propose a sustainability initiative involving a business, an NGO, and a local community.

L6
Definition
A tri-sector 'Clean Lake & Green Livelihoods' initiative unites corporate CSR funding, NGO technical expertise, and local community stewardship.
Key Point
The business funds sewage interception and solar aerators, the NGO trains residents and monitors water quality, and the community maintains the lakefront and runs eco-trails.
Example
An IT company funding the revival of a Pune urban lake, an environmental NGO restoring native wetlands, and local residents forming a lake-watch committee.
Source: JSPM University Pune, School of Civil and Environmental Sciences — Environment and Sustainability Question Bank (231GCEB02, 120 Questions).
